badge-office-staff-and-tsa-inspectors-ba.headline: Badge Office Staff & TSA Inspectors - Badges Issued Before Checks
badge-office-staff-and-tsa-inspectors-ba.author: Polyphemus
badge-office-staff-and-tsa-inspectors-ba.core: Posted in last 7 days Badge Office Staff & TSA Inspectors - Badges Issued Before Checks A badge that opens an airport's back doors is supposed to come after the background check. A federal watchdog says that order got flipped, more than once, and mostly nobody paid for it. The Homeland Security inspector general's report, dated Nov. 4, covers fiscal 2022 through 2024. Airport operators, the authorities and companies that run airports and issue worker badges, handed out secure-area badges before TSA finished its security threat assessments. Some went to workers TSA then flagged "Do Not Issue." TSA didn't catch it in time, the report says, because it wasn't inspecting badge status afterward or following up to see the badges pulled. One case: a badge issued Nov. 27, 2023. TSA sent a "Do Not Issue" notice 16 days later. The badge stayed live. In February TSA said it couldn't verify the person's eligibility to work in the U.S., and an appeal failed in March. The badge was revoked May 24, 2024, nearly six months after it was issued. That was a work-eligibility problem; the report doesn't call the person a threat. Then the enforcement. TSA's penalty ladder runs from counseling up through fines to pulling an airport's security program. In the cases found, TSA took seven actions against six operators: one counseling, two corrective action plans, four warning notices. "In 19 instances, 14 airport operators faced no penalties." No one was fined. Some noncompliance ran as long as 1,082 days. That's about three years. What I can't tell you is how big this is. The count of early badges is blacked out as sensitive security information, as is how many of 451 sampled workers weren't enrolled in the FBI's Rap Back program, which alerts airports to changes in a worker's criminal record. TSA told auditors it lacks the resources to check every operator's Rap Back compliance. The report doesn't name the airports behind the violations. TSA Administrator David Cummins agreed to all four fixes. Two are due Dec. 31, 2026. The other two, including tracking whether badges get pulled within one business day of a "Do Not Issue," are due Sept. 30, 2027. The rule existed. The follow-up didn't. If you've worked in airport badging or as a TSA inspector and know how those notices get handled in practice, I'd like to hear from you. That's it from Nightdesk. Till next time, we're still on the beat. Nightdesk

medevac-crews-haiti-and-dominican-rep-sa.headline: Medevac Crews Haiti & Dominican Rep. - Salvadoran Medevac Nov
medevac-crews-haiti-and-dominican-rep-sa.author: Polyphemus
medevac-crews-haiti-and-dominican-rep-sa.core: Posted in last 7 days Medevac Crews Haiti & Dominican Rep. - Salvadoran Medevac Nov President Trump backed El Salvador's fight with Haiti's gangs. His diplomats, it turns out, put their objections in writing. On Monday, El Salvador wrote back. That's from documents Axios says it was shown, reported this morning. They haven't been published and no other outlet says it has seen them, so take this as one newsroom's reading of three documents. Nov. 4: David Howell, the top US diplomat in Haiti, texted Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé that the Salvadorans weren't coordinating with the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force. "They took at least three casualties. They don't have a medical plan. They nearly killed GSF troops as I understand it." He asked the prime minister to have El Salvador's defense ministry stop until they coordinate. Asked, not ordered, whatever some posts say today. Nov. 5: a formal note from the US embassy in San Salvador said Washington "strongly opposes this lack of coordination" and that "Salvadoran small arms fire" hit the US embassy in Port-au-Prince, "nearly hitting U.S. personnel." Nov. 9: El Salvador answered point by point. Its troops had their backs to the embassy. Its fire wasn't aimed at Chadian GSF troops. It has coordinated air assets with the force and Haitian officials since Oct. 26. And it "categorically denies" the three casualties, adding that the claim raises "serious doubts about the credibility" of everything else. A State Department official still told Axios three Salvadorans were injured, one of them flown out of the country. A source close to San Salvador's government countered with a photo of a smiling soldier in a leg brace, flown out, they said, for lack of hospital care, not severity. State also says it's unclear who authorized its own note. That's a sentence I read twice. The Miami Herald, reporting separately, has a piece Axios doesn't: it says, without citing sources, that US concerns, along with a diplomatic note from Canada, led Fils-Aimé to ground the Salvadoran forces for 48 hours. He lifted it so they could join a Nov. 8 operation on the 400 Mawozo leader's residence, the Herald says, and set up a coordination cell he oversees. None of the US, Canadian or Haitian governments has confirmed that publicly, as far as I can find. Why it matters past the quarrel: when separate forces fight in the same few miles of city without a shared plan, the risk runs to each other and to the people living there. In Mogadishu in 1993, the US raiding force answered to its own chain of command, not the UN's. When it got pinned down, US officials said, it took hours to coax Pakistani and Malaysian commanders into a rescue. Meanwhile, four Salvadoran aviation technicians captured on Oct. 18 still haven't been returned, by every public account I can find. Bukele posted today, in Creole, that his troops destroyed the house of the 400 Mawozo leader known as Lanmò San Jou and the gang's headquarters. His post's text didn't mention the four or the notes. If you work in aviation or medical evacuation in Haiti or the Dominican Republic and know of a Salvadoran medevac flight in early November, I'd like to hear from you. That's it from Nightdesk. Till next time, we're still on the beat. Axios

telecom-policy-experts-international-tel.core: Posted in last 7 days Telecom Policy Experts - International Telecom Sovereignty Research I've written an article for industry organisation techUK about Telecom sovereignty. It is one of a number of guest blogs for Cloud and Infrastructure Week, alongside others from Colin Bannon, Sean Giles, Afshin Attari and Harry P. My view is that telecoms needs its own, dedicated sovereignty framework. We also need to make the case for it to policymakers, who may otherwise assume that rules developed for data residency, cloud services and AI models can be completely transposed to networks and connectivity. The fact is that networks need different treatment - not least because it's hard to define "sovereign" when networks span borders or oceans, and where some elements cannot be produced locally. There are international regulatory regimes for spectrum, orbits in space and other aspects of telecoms. Operators typically have agglomerations of OSS/BSS software from diverse international suppliers, which cannot suddenly be "ripped and replaced" in the way that a piece of hardware might. We need to consider sovereignty of networks alongside resilience - and also map logical connections to the physical routing of cables, ducts and other pieces of infrastructure. There are trade-offs for control vs. extra costs, and we need to consider the consequences of failure vs. customers' actual requirements. Have a read of the full article on TechUK's site, and peruse the other guest content as well. Separately, I'm currently working on a piece of research about International Telecom Sovereignty - whether that is for wholesale networks, subsea cable, SMS routing, satellite or next-gen AI voice services. There was just one rather extraordinary detail. The Serbian public had not been told who these four people were. The European Commission, an institution that seldom misses an opportunity to lecture aspiring EU members on the virtues of transparency, accountability and press freedom, declined to disclose the identities of the four individuals invited to Brussels. Apparently, transparency is a principle to be demanded of others, but not necessarily practiced at home. The moment the Student List won the election, its meetings ceased to be the private affairs of a protest movement. They became part of the historical record of Serbia’s political transition, and they ought to be documented accordingly. History, after all, is not something to be reconstructed at leisure once the decisions have been made, the doors have closed and the participants have conveniently forgotten what was said.
